episode_title: 90 minutes of unfiltered product advice from Snap and Discord’s product chief | Peter Sellis
description_html:
Peter Sellis was the first product manager at Snapchat, where he spent seven years building one of the most beloved consumer products in history. He went on to serve as Head of Product at Discord, where he helped drive some of the fastest user growth the platform had seen. Having left his role at Discord, he gets to be especially real and unfiltered — nothing to promote, no PR, no comms team.

In our in-depth conversation, we discuss:

1. Why Peter designs teams like . . . terrorist organizations

2. What it was really like to manage Nikita Bier

3. Why the median PM is so bad

4. Why Snapchat’s ads business never reached its potential

5. Why growth almost always comes from the core product

6. Peter’s three “oxymorons” of great product management

—

summary.overview: Peter Sellis, former first PM at Snapchat and head of product at Discord, shares candid lessons about product leadership, team design, growth, monetization, taste, and ambition. He argues for highly autonomous teams with clear ideological alignment, concentrating responsibility on exceptional people, improving core product usage before expanding, and building the restraint to say no—even as AI makes creation easier.

takeaways.heading: Teams as networks
takeaways.detail: Sellis designs teams around two principles: a shared, almost religious understanding of the mission and a clear structure for who can make which decisions. Reducing collaboration is intentional because coordination costs can make the whole organization move at the speed of its slowest node.

takeaways.heading: Handling unusual talent
takeaways.detail: Organizations should be able to accommodate highly “spiky” talent, such as Nikita Bier, rather than forcing everyone into a standard employee mold. Sellis compares Bier to Liam Neeson in Taken: extraordinarily effective in his specialty, but not someone to manage conventionally.

takeaways.heading: Why PMs can be harmful
takeaways.detail: Sellis says product-management ability has a power-law distribution: excellent PMs often leave to become founders or executives, while mediocre PMs have strong incentives to remain. He also observes that great engineers usually avoid bad PMs or know how to extract value from them, so complaints often come from people in the middle.

takeaways.heading: Spend time on winners
takeaways.detail: Rather than rescuing people who are struggling, Sellis gives strong performers more responsibility until they begin making bad decisions. He publicly defends his team and uses increasing responsibility as a way to demonstrate trust, while acknowledging that he has limited mechanisms for improving weaker performers.

takeaways.heading: Snapchat’s monetization limits
takeaways.detail: Sellis identifies three structural challenges for Snapchat’s advertising business: its especially young audience is harder to measure and target, the camera-first experience offers no obvious place for ads, and messaging products generally lack strong ad formats. He says Snapchat’s subscription product has been successful, but might have helped more if launched several years earlier.

takeaways.heading: Snapchat’s product breadth
takeaways.detail: Despite its monetization constraints, Sellis describes Snapchat as the leading messaging, camera, maps, and astrology product for many young users in Western countries. He argues that its consumer-product track record deserves study even though it did not become the next Facebook.

takeaways.heading: Say no with taste
takeaways.detail: Sellis saw Evan Spiegel reject better ideas than many consumer startups ever launch. He compares a product leader to a museum curator: if everything in the collection is displayed, the curator has not exercised judgment.

takeaways.heading: Model systems mathematically
takeaways.detail: Sellis says systems thinking is more useful when expressed through variables, stocks, flows, distributions, and levers rather than reduced to repeatedly asking “why.” He recommends modeling a system in a spreadsheet, even if the model never goes beyond the team’s shared drive.

takeaways.heading: Ads in AI products
takeaways.detail: Sellis believes advertising remains a powerful internet business model and says OpenAI is rapidly adopting the right advertising infrastructure. In chat, he thinks the key auction variable may be trust: ads should not undermine the user’s confidence in answers, and the format will become especially challenging in voice.

takeaways.heading: Return to the core
takeaways.detail: Sellis argues that growth often comes from existing users rather than new markets. At Snapchat, improving Android performance after the 2018 redesign helped restart growth; at Discord, focusing on making gaming with friends better drove growth even though gamers already appeared to have near-total penetration.

takeaways.heading: When to expand
takeaways.detail: He suggests expanding through adjacent cohorts that can benefit from the product’s core strength, or by following unexpected ways users already go through extra effort to use the product. A more ambitious approach is “backcasting”: envisioning the best future version of the product without being constrained by today’s technology.

takeaways.heading: Building for the future
takeaways.detail: Sellis cites SpaceX’s willingness to move beyond the highly successful Falcon 9 toward Starship as an example of avoiding the innovator’s dilemma. He also admires how SpaceX and Tesla have publicly articulated long-term plans and then executed against them.

takeaways.heading: Great PM contradictions
takeaways.detail: Sellis describes three pairs of traits in great PMs: confidence balanced by humility, strong organization balanced by comfort with ambiguity, and long-term thinking balanced by an urgent bias for action. The best PMs can set the pace of a team while keeping a distant goal in view.

takeaways.heading: Core product value
takeaways.detail: At Snap and Discord, Sellis translated the product’s mission into short phrases tied to measurable behaviors. Examples were Snapchat as “the fastest way to share a moment with the people you care about” and Discord as “the best way to talk and hang out with your friends before, during, and after playing games.”

takeaways.heading: Long-term greedy
takeaways.detail: For advertising businesses, Sellis advocates being “long-term greedy”: prioritize advertiser ROI today, even when that may reduce short-term revenue, because sustainable revenue depends on advertisers continuing to see value and increasing their budgets.

takeaways.heading: Personal contrarian views
takeaways.detail: Sellis says choosing a life partner is one of the most consequential career decisions, that people with taste often stop one step before something becomes gauche or “cringe,” and that certain consumer products may benefit from product teams whose lived backgrounds give them an unusually strong understanding of particular human needs.

takeaways.heading: Time and experience
takeaways.detail: Sellis is motivated by the idea that “from nothing to nothing is no time at all.” He believes experiencing more, meeting people, and acting on meaningful opportunities can make life feel fuller rather than allowing time to pass without signposts.

quotes.text: Collaboration comes with incredible coordination costs, and coordination costs essentially assure that you're moving as slow as the slowest node in the system.
quotes.speaker: Peter Sellis
